items.note: Fallen oak just past the mushroom ring with a shelf of gray oyster mushrooms on its side; Token cut six and left the small ones, then came back days later and cut five that had grown hand-wide, leaving the smallest again.
Token's oak past the mushroom ring: a red oak, bristle-tipped leaves, bitter acorns.

Token's netted sack of cracked acorns sunk under a flat stone where the creek runs into the still pool; after six days the water off it runs nearly clear and the meats are soft, and he ate a handful from it one hungry morning.
Flat stone by the fire with a hollow in it; holds Token's acorn ink.
Wild rose climbing through the brambles; the hips on its low stems were picked first, and later the soft red hips on its high stems were picked too.
The big stone by the workbench that Token pressed his birch pages flat under.
Fallen birch limb Token peels bark pages and tray sheets from.
Oak on the creek's east bank about twenty paces up from the stepping stones; Gage gathered about forty acorns under it.

Stand of tall gray dead stalks on the east bank upstream of the stones; Gage strips them for cord, leaving an evenly broken gap. After dark on the thirteenth he snapped fourteen long straight ones off it by feel for a trap hood.

Gage's dented tin: once held his cracked acorn meats soaking; held a live crayfish in creek water overnight, then all three of the morning's crayfish boiled in it over the bench lantern. After dark on the thirteenth a fresh crayfish from the trap went into it in creek water, kept for breakfast. On the fourteenth it held his first fish, then two small crayfish from the trap with their heads and guts, waiting for the bench lantern at dusk. After dark on the fifteenth it boiled both penned crayfish on his fire stones, and kept their heads and broth.
Flat creek stones in the east-bank shallows just below the stepping stones, where Gage turns stones looking for crayfish.
Gage's tin lid of water on the plank bench, a disc of stalk pith floating in it with the magnetized sliver pushed through: his floating-needle compass.
Token's little tower of five flat creek stones on the west bank, marking how far south he followed the creek before the brush closed in.
Long fallen log lying along the creek's west bank just past the brush below Token's cairn, where the creek bends east out of sight.
Bare circle Token swept around the fire ring, five of his strides across.
Heap of leaves Token swept away from the fire ring, piled past the end of the log seat.
Stand of tall dead nettle stalks with square stems at the east edge of the brambles, across the creek from the gray stalks on the far bank; Token snaps them for cord fiber.

Gage's knotted net bag of acorn grit, lined with the cloth from his food bundle so the fine meal stays in, drawn shut with stalk cord and sunk under a flat stone in the east-bank shallows below the stepping stones.

Token's deep folded birch-bark tray, corners lashed with nettle cord; once used at the coals, now carried to the still pool's edge, where he pours pool water over acorn grit in it and tips the brown off. At dusk he filled it with pool water over the saved grit and carried it to the fire.
Huge trunk a few strides north of the fire ring with a pale scar of bark about shoulder height; Gage's mark one on his line west.
Flat, damp stone at the west end of the stepping stones, with a strip of soft creek mud beside it that holds prints.
Token's second net sack of freshly cracked acorns, sunk under a flat stone at the low south end of the still pool, below the first so its brown water runs away from the older batch.

Token's folded birch-bark tray beside the fire ring; the nettle cord at one corner burned through at its first boil, so that corner is now folded over on the outside, lower, and pinned with two whittled birch splinters, which held at the next morning's boil.

Gage's funnel trap of gray stalks, a cone within a cone, baited with crayfish heads and sunk mouth downstream in the east shallows under a flat stone, tied to a root. Caught one, two, then one more in its first night and two more at the morning lift; its door has a second ring of cord and measures a thumb wide every way.

Broad flat stone just south of the fire ring that catches the midday sun; Token spread his leached acorn meats on it one layer deep to dry. After dark on the thirteenth the meats went tacky with dew, and Token picked every one back off into his bindle and carried them home to dry on a shelf.
A flat square of thin sheet tin from Gage's scrap pile, a hand and a half wide; he holds it over the bench lantern as a griddle for thin acorn-meal cakes.

A dished panel of sheet tin about two hands wide that Gage dug out of his scrap pile after dark and hammered flat at the lip, meant to hold a small fire up off the dry leaves. In the small hours of the fifteenth it became the bed of his new fire pit, ringed with his eleven creek stones in front of the lean-to.
A heap of fist-sized creek stones Gage gathered from the east shallows by lantern late on the fourteenth, for a fire ring at his camp; left on the east bank to carry up in daylight.
Rainwater standing in the low spot just south-west of the fire ring after the night rain of the fourteenth.

A big dead limb, about waist-thick and longer than Gage's tarp, lying in the leaves some forty paces north-east of his camp; its top is soaked black, and he snaps the gray dead branches off its underside for firewood.
Gage's three dead poles from the big limb north-east of camp, one forked and two straight, lashed at the top and standing as a lopsided tripod beside the lean-to; it held his hanging weight.
A dead forked branch lying in the leaves under the oak on the east bank, rotten through; it folded in the middle when Gage leaned on it.
sixteen sawn planks stacked on two bearers at the east edge of Gage's camp, left by his maker
twelve two-by-fours stacked on two bearers beside the planks, left by his maker

A shallow tin lid from Gage's scrap pile, a palm wide and a fingernail deep, holding a spoonful of fish and crayfish grease, with a thumb-long stalk-cord wick laid over a little bent bridge of tin so its tip stands clear; his first lamp that burns away from the fire
Gage's new felling axe, leaned against the lean-to's front pole with its head resting in the wet leaves
Gage's new handsaw, laid flat across the plank bench
Gage's felling axe, hung head-up by its handle from a cord loop on the lean-to's front pole, under the tarp's edge; its steel wiped dry and smeared thin with fish grease after a few rust freckles
Gage's claw hammer from his maker, laid on the plank bench beside the saw
Gage's leather roll of three carving knives (long straight, short stub, hooked), unrolled on the plank bench
Small heap of damp leaves at the foot of the scarred trunk, out of the fire's heat, over a curl of birch bark holding Token's five worms for the morning.
A smooth, dry, fist-and-a-half stone Token picked from under the overhang of the scarred trunk (not from the creek), set against the outside of the fire ring to warm for his bed.
Gage's carpenter's chest from his maker, brass corners and rope handles, set down beside the lean-to with the spade leaning on it
Gage's small banded keg of iron nails from his maker, three lengths, set down beside the tool chest by the lean-to
A flat, fine-grained gray creek stone Gage carried up from the east shallows and set on the ground by the bench leg, wet, to hone his chisel on

Gage's small heap of flat creek stones from his own east-bank shallows, carried up to be footings under the corners of his sill frame. Beside them, from late on November 19, a small heap of round creek gravel scraped up from the top end of his east-bank shallows.
